beats.text: On the disk, a program is just a file. It does nothing. It is passive.
Run it, and it becomes a process: a program in execution. Active, with its own memory and its own state.
Its memory has four parts. Text holds the code. Data holds the global variables.
The heap grows up when the program asks for memory. The stack grows down with every function call.
One program can be several processes at once, like two windows of the same browser.
Now follow one process through its life.
It is born in the new state. Once admitted, it moves to ready, and waits in line for a CPU.
The scheduler dispatches it. Now it is running.
A timer interrupt stops it. Back to ready.
Dispatched again, it asks the disk for data. Now it is waiting. It could not use the CPU anyway.
The disk finishes. Does the process jump straight back onto the CPU?
No. Waiting goes to ready, never straight to running. Only the scheduler moves a process from ready to running.
At last it calls exit, and terminates. Five states, six arrows.
To pause a process and resume it later, the OS keeps a process control block for it: its state, its I D, its program counter, its registers, and more.
A context switch saves the running process into its P C B, and loads the next one from its own.
During the switch, no useful work gets done. It is pure overhead.
How is a new process born? With fork. fork makes a copy of the calling process, and both carry on from the same point.
The only difference is the return value. The parent gets the child's P I D. The child gets zero.
Then exec replaces the child's program with a new one, like ls. Same process, new code.
If every process calls fork three times in a row, you get two to the power three: eight processes.
Processes can also talk: through a shared memory area, or by sending messages through the kernel.
For the exam.
A program is passive, a process is active.
Five states, six transitions.
Waiting never goes straight to running.
The P C B saves a process; switching is overhead.
fork returns zero to the child, the P I D to the parent.
